At Old Down, Woodpigeons feed in the open grassland and field edges, and roost and nest in the hedgerows and scrub. They are an important prey item for Peregrine Falcon, which hunts over the site, and for Goshawk in nearby woodland. Large flocks gather on farmland near the site in autumn to feed on harvested fields.
native_info: Abundant resident throughout the UK. Found in almost all habitats with trees or hedgerows. Has increased significantly in population since the 1960s. One of Britain's most common birds.
wildlife_value: Major prey item for Peregrine Falcon, Goshawk, and Sparrowhawk. Seeds passed through the gut are dispersed widely. Nest sites used by other species. Provides a substantial food source for raptors — the presence of large Woodpigeon flocks near Old Down partly explains the regular Red Kite and occasional Peregrine sightings.

life_stages.description: Large, heavy-bodied pigeon with blue-grey plumage. The white neck patches are the most distinctive feature — white crescents on each side of the neck with iridescent green-purple plumage below them. The breast is pinkish-grey. In flight, white wing bars flash across each wing. Eyes are pale yellow.

photos.caption: Woodpigeon adult showing the distinctive white neck patches

life_stages.description: Young Woodpigeons lack the white neck patches entirely and are slightly duller brown-grey overall. They are often seen in summer following adults and begging for food. The white neck patches develop gradually through the first autumn.

photos.caption: Fledgling Woodpigeon — no white neck patch yet, scruffier plumage
Young Woodpigeon — juvenile plumage before the white neck patch develops

similar_species.similarity_note: Both medium-large grey pigeons in similar habitats
similar_species.key_difference: Stock Dove is smaller and compact, with no white neck patches and no white wing bars. It has two small black wing bars instead. Frequents old trees with nest holes; less common than Woodpigeon.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Both present year-round

photos.caption: Woodpigeon — the largest and most common UK pigeon
Woodpigeon — the large white neck patch and pink breast are the best ID features
Woodpigeon perched — note the iridescent green and purple neck sheen
Fledgling Woodpigeon — no white neck patch yet, scruffier plumage

summary: One of the most ecologically important animals at Old Down — rabbits graze the chalk grassland short, which is exactly what rare wildflowers and butterflies need to survive. Without rabbits, coarser grasses would take over and the delicate chalk grassland plants would be smothered. Look for their warrens in the sunny slope banks.
full_description:
The Rabbit (Oryctolagus cuniculus) was introduced to Britain by the Normans around 1100 AD and is now so thoroughly naturalised that it functions as a native species ecologically. At 40–50cm long, rabbits are easily recognised — brown-grey fur, long ears with black tips, large hind legs, and the distinctive white 'scut' (tail) that flashes as they flee. They are most active at dawn and dusk, though visible throughout the day at undisturbed sites like Old Down.

Rabbits are ecosystem engineers at Old Down. By grazing the chalk grassland very short and evenly, they prevent coarser, more competitive grasses from overwhelming the fine-leaved chalk grassland species that rare plants and butterflies depend on. Without rabbit grazing, the grassland at Old Down would gradually be colonised by rank grass, then Bramble and Hawthorn scrub, and the chalk grassland community — including Cowslip, Bird's-foot Trefoil, Small Blue butterfly, and Marbled White — would decline and eventually disappear. Myxomatosis can severely reduce rabbit populations, and when this happens the grassland quality changes noticeably within a few years.

Signs of rabbits are easy to find at Old Down. Warrens — networks of burrows — are visible as holes 10–20cm across with fresh-dug soil around the entrance, often on south-facing slopes where the chalk is near the surface. Round black droppings (about 1cm across) are scattered widely, often in latrine piles. Grazing marks on plants — clean-angled cuts on grass stems and shrub shoots — are also characteristic. Rabbits are important prey for Red Kite, Buzzard, Stoat, Fox, and Kestrel on the site.
native_info: Introduced to Britain by the Normans c.1100 AD. Now fully naturalised and one of the most widespread mammals in the UK. Most abundant on chalk, limestone, and sandy soils where burrowing is easy.
wildlife_value: Critical ecosystem engineer for chalk grassland — grazing maintains the short, diverse sward that rare plants and butterflies depend on at Old Down. Burrows provide shelter for other species including Rabbits obviously, but also Shelduck, Bumblebee queens, and various invertebrates. Major prey species for Red Kite, Buzzard, Kestrel, Fox, Stoat, and Weasel.

life_stages.description: Brown-grey fur above with pale buff underside; large ears 7–8cm long; powerful hind legs; white 'scut' (tail) that flashes when the animal runs. The white tail is a warning signal to other rabbits. Eyes are large and positioned on the sides of the head, giving a wide field of vision. Look for them in the early morning and evening, sitting up and alert before moving to feed.

photos.caption: Rabbit on chalk grassland — a key ecosystem engineer at Old Down
European Rabbit — brown-grey adult showing characteristic large ears
Rabbit showing alert posture and white tail (scut)

life_stages.description: Warrens are systems of interconnected burrows with entrance holes 10–20cm across, usually on sunny slopes or in hedgerow banks. Fresh soil (spoil) at the entrance indicates active use. Round dark droppings, about 1cm across, are scattered widely around the warren and in latrine piles on prominent spots. Gnawed grass and bark at ground level shows where rabbits have been feeding. Footprints show large hind feet landing in front of the smaller front feet.

Young rabbits (called kittens or kits) are born underground from February onwards and emerge at about 3 weeks old. They are miniature versions of adults but rounder, slightly fluffier, and with proportionally larger ears and eyes. Several litters are produced each year — rabbits can breed rapidly when conditions are good.

similar_species.similarity_note: Both medium-sized brown mammals with long ears in open grassland
similar_species.key_difference: Brown Hare is much larger (50–70cm), with longer black-tipped ears, longer hind legs, and a distinctly black-and-white tail (black on top, white below). Hares live entirely above ground — no warrens — and rely on speed. Hares have a wilder, more powerful look than Rabbits.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Both present year-round; Hares are less common at Old Down than Rabbits

photos.caption: Rabbit — essential grazer of Old Down's chalk grassland
European Rabbit adult portrait
Rabbit showing the white scut (tail) that flashes as a warning signal

confidence_note: Buff-tailed Bumblebee can be confused with White-tailed Bumblebee (Bombus lucorum), which is very similar but has a cleaner white tail and brighter lemon-yellow bands. The tail colour — buff-orange vs white — is the key difference, but is not always easy to judge in the field.
summary: One of Britain's largest and most important bumblebees. The queen emerges in early spring — sometimes even in January in mild winters — and is enormous compared to other insects at that time of year. Watch Cowslips and Knapweed flowers at Old Down for the constant movement of workers collecting pollen and nectar.
full_description:
The Buff-tailed Bumblebee (Bombus terrestris) is one of the most abundant and widespread bumblebees in Britain. Queens are very large — up to 22mm long — with a yellow band on the thorax, a second yellow band on the abdomen, and a buff-orange tail. Workers are similar but smaller (11–17mm). Males are smaller still, with a more extensive yellow pattern and a yellow-tipped face. The tail colour varies and can be quite pale in worn individuals, making separation from the White-tailed Bumblebee tricky in the field.

Queen Buff-tailed Bumblebees are among the very first insects to emerge in spring, sometimes flying in January or February in mild weather. After hibernating in a small underground cell, the queen must feed intensively to build up energy reserves before finding a suitable nest site — typically an old mouse hole, compost heap, or underground cavity. She then builds a colony of 200–400 workers through spring and summer, which fan out to forage across a large area. A single worker will visit thousands of flowers per day.

At Old Down, Buff-tailed Bumblebees are among the key pollinators of Cowslip, Bird's-foot Trefoil, Knapweed, and Bramble. Their workers also visit Red Clover, Vetch species, and a wide range of other flowers. Other bumblebee species also occur at Old Down, including the Red-tailed Bumblebee (Bombus lapidarius) — unmistakable with an all-black body and red tail — and the Early Bumblebee (Bombus pratorum), which is smaller and has an orange tail even earlier in the year.
danger_note: Female bumblebees can sting if handled or if their nest is disturbed, but are not aggressive when foraging on flowers. Unlike honey bees, bumblebees can sting multiple times. Leave nests undisturbed.
native_info: Native throughout England, Wales, and southern Scotland. One of Britain's most common bumblebees, present in almost all habitats from gardens to chalk grassland. Colony size 200–400 workers.
wildlife_value: One of the most important pollinators in Britain, visiting a huge range of wildflowers. Essential for the pollination of Bramble, White Clover, Bird's-foot Trefoil, and many other plants at Old Down. The long-tongued workers can reach nectar in deeper flowers including Cowslip. Colonies provide food for Badgers who excavate nests for larvae and honeypot stores.

life_stages.description: The queen is the first sign of Buff-tailed Bumblebee in the year — a large, heavy bee appearing in February–April, flying low over the ground looking for a nest site, or feeding intensively on early flowers like Willowherb, Dandelion, and Blackthorn. She is noticeably larger than any worker bee. One yellow band on the thorax, one on the abdomen, and a buff-orange tail.

photos.caption: Buff-tailed Bumblebee queen foraging — note the large size and buff tail

life_stages.description: Workers are much smaller than the queen but share the same yellow-and-buff pattern. They visit flowers constantly, often carrying visible orange pollen baskets (corbiculae) on their hind legs. Watch a Knapweed or Bramble flower at Old Down and workers will pass through every few seconds on a warm day.

photos.caption: Buff-tailed Bumblebee worker on a flower

similar_species.similarity_note: Very similar species, often in the same habitat
similar_species.key_difference: White-tailed Bumblebee (Bombus lucorum) has a pure white tail (vs buff-orange), brighter lemon-yellow bands, and is generally slightly smaller. The difference in tail colour can be subtle in faded or worn individuals. Both species occur at Old Down.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Both fly February–October

similar_species.similarity_note: Another common bumblebee at Old Down
similar_species.key_difference: Red-tailed Bumblebee (Bombus lapidarius) is completely distinctive — all-black body with a vivid red-orange tail. No yellow bands on the thorax or abdomen.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Red-tailed Bumblebee flies April–September

photos.caption: Buff-tailed Bumblebee queen — note large size and buff-orange tail
Buff-tailed Bumblebee worker foraging

confidence_note: Males are unmistakable — electric bright blue with black border and white fringe. Females are mostly brown with variable blue scales near the body and orange spots near the wing margin, and can be confused with Brown Argus or Small Blue females. Both sexes have diagnostic orange spots on the undersides of all wings.
summary: The male is an electric metallic blue that seems to glow in sunlight — one of the most beautiful sights of British grassland summer. Both sexes have lovely orange-spotted undersides. The caterpillars feed on Bird's-foot Trefoil, so finding the butterfly at Old Down means the chalk grassland is in good shape.
full_description:
The Common Blue (Polyommatus icarus) is the most widespread blue butterfly in Britain and among the most beautiful. Males have vivid sky-blue upperwings with a narrow black border and white fringe, and seem to glow in sunlight — a blue that is almost impossible to describe in writing. Females are predominantly brown with variable amounts of blue near the wing base and orange spots along the outer margins. Both sexes share the same distinctive underside: pale grey-buff with black spots and a row of vivid orange-red spots near the wing margins — this pattern is the reliable ID feature for both sexes.

The Common Blue has two broods at Old Down in a good year — the first flies May to June, the second July to September. The caterpillars feed primarily on Bird's-foot Trefoil (Lotus corniculatus), with some use of related legumes. Eggs are laid singly on the upper surface of trefoil leaflets. The caterpillars are green and well-camouflaged, and are tended by ants — the caterpillars have a special gland that produces a liquid the ants drink, and in return the ants protect the caterpillar from predators.

At Old Down, Common Blue is typically more numerous than Small Blue, and is a strong indicator of chalk grassland quality. On warm sunny days in July, it is possible to see males spiralling upward in territorial chases, females nectaring on Knapweed and Marjoram, and both sexes roosting with wings closed on tall grass stems in the evening.
native_info: Native throughout the UK. The most common and widespread blue butterfly in Britain. Most abundant on chalk and limestone grassland, coastal dunes, and brownfield sites where Bird's-foot Trefoil grows.
wildlife_value: Caterpillars are specifically dependent on Bird's-foot Trefoil, making this butterfly a reliable indicator of good chalk grassland. Caterpillars are tended by ants — a mutualistic relationship. Adults are prey for spiders and birds. The presence of Common Blue at Old Down indicates a healthy population of its food plant.

life_stages.description: Eggs are tiny, disc-shaped, and pale green-white, laid singly on the upper surface of Bird's-foot Trefoil leaflets. They are very difficult to spot without a hand lens. Newly hatched caterpillars eat the egg shell before starting on the leaf.

Green, slug-like caterpillar with a darker line along the back and pale sides — excellent camouflage on the trefoil leaves. Look for small black ants attending the caterpillar: the caterpillar has a gland on its back that produces a sweet secretion that ants drink, and the ants guard the caterpillar in return.

Electric sky-blue upperwings with a narrow black border and white fringe. The blue has a slightly violet tone in certain lights. Underwing is pale buff-grey with black spots and vivid orange spots near the margin. Males are territorial and can be seen chasing other males on sunny days.

photos.caption: Common Blue male upperside — the vivid electric blue is unmistakable on a sunny day
Common Blue showing diagnostic orange-spotted underside

life_stages.description: Brown upperwings with variable amounts of blue scaling near the wing base (some females are almost as blue as males, others almost entirely brown). Orange spots along the outer wing margin. The orange-spotted underside is the same as the male and is the most reliable identification feature.

photos.caption: Common Blue mating pair — male (blue, left) and female (brown, right)

similar_species.similarity_note: Both blue butterflies occurring at Old Down
similar_species.key_difference: Small Blue is much smaller with a wingspan of 16–27mm (Common Blue 28–36mm). Male Small Blue is not blue — it is sooty grey-brown with a dusting of blue scales near the body. Underside is pale grey with black dots and NO orange spots.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Both fly May–August at Old Down

similar_species.similarity_note: Another blue butterfly sometimes seen at Old Down
similar_species.key_difference: Holly Blue underside is distinctive — plain silvery-blue with tiny black dots and no orange spots. Holly Blue flies earlier in spring (April) and tends to fly high around Holly and Ivy, rather than low over grassland.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Holly Blue first brood April–May; Common Blue May–September

photos.caption: Common Blue male — one of Old Down's most beautiful summer butterflies
Common Blue showing the diagnostic orange-spotted underside
Common Blue mating pair — male blue (left), female brown (right)

summary: One of Britain's most abundant grassland butterflies, and one of the few that will fly on dull, overcast days. Old Down can be carpeted with Meadow Browns in July and August. The single large eye-spot on the forewing is the key ID feature.
full_description:
The Meadow Brown (Maniola jurtina) is Britain's most abundant butterfly by population, and one of the most characteristic species of summer grassland. Males are dark brown with a small orange patch on the forewing containing a single black eye-spot with a white centre. Females are larger with a more extensive orange-brown patch on the forewing and a more prominent eye-spot. The underside of the hindwing is mottled buff-brown with a small cluster of spots — much paler and less patterned than many browns.

The Meadow Brown is unusual among British butterflies in that it will fly in overcast and even light rain, unlike most species that only fly in sunshine. This makes it one of the most reliably visible butterflies on visits to Old Down through the summer. It is single-brooded — one flight period from June through September — and the adults live for several weeks, nectaring on Knapweed, Bramble, Marjoram, and many other flowers. The caterpillars feed on a range of fine grasses, which is why the species thrives in both chalk grassland and rough grassland habitats.

At Old Down, Meadow Brown is typically the most numerous butterfly by count in summer, often hundreds visible simultaneously on a warm July day. It makes an excellent species for children learning to count butterflies — it is abundant, easy to spot, and lands frequently on flowers. Look especially on Knapweed, Bramble flowers, and Ragwort.
native_info: Native throughout England, Wales, and Ireland. One of the most abundant butterflies in Britain. Found in almost all grassland habitats, from chalk downland to coastal dunes to roadside verges.
wildlife_value: Caterpillars feed on common fine grasses, making this butterfly independent of specialist plants and very adaptable. Adults are important pollinators of Knapweed, Bramble, and Marjoram. Prey for bats, spiders, and birds. The abundance of Meadow Brown at Old Down provides a baseline indicator for grassland quality that is easy to monitor.

life_stages.description: The caterpillar hibernates over winter as a small larva, resuming feeding in spring on fine grasses. It is green with a pale stripe along each side, well camouflaged in the grass stems. By May it has grown to full size and pupates in a chrysalis close to the ground.

Dark brown wings with a small orange-brown patch on the upper forewing and a single black eye-spot (with one or two white pupils). Males tend to be darker than females. The underside of the hindwing is mottled brown and buff — much plainer than the Gatekeeper.

photos.caption: Meadow Brown male showing the dark brown wings and eye-spot on forewing

life_stages.description: Females are slightly larger than males with a more extensive orange-brown band on the forewing and a more prominent eye-spot. The orange colouring makes females look warmer and brighter than males when settled on a flower. Both sexes rest with wings closed when not in active flight.

photos.caption: Meadow Brown female — orange colouring more extensive than male

similar_species.similarity_note: Very similar brown butterfly often in the same habitat
similar_species.key_difference: Gatekeeper (Pyronia tithonus) is smaller, with two white pupils in the eye-spot (Meadow Brown has one or two but usually one), more orange on the forewing, and a distinctly patterned underside of the hindwing (Meadow Brown's is plainer). Gatekeeper prefers scrub-grassland edges and hedgerows rather than open grassland.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Gatekeeper flies July–August; Meadow Brown June–September

similar_species.similarity_note: Another brown grassland butterfly that can occur at Old Down
similar_species.key_difference: Ringlet is darker brown, almost sooty, with multiple cream-ringed eyespots on the underside of both wings. Meadow Brown is warmer brown with much plainer hindwing underside.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Ringlet flies June–August; Meadow Brown June–September

photos.caption: Meadow Brown — Britain's most abundant grassland butterfly
Meadow Brown male showing single eye-spot on dark forewing

confidence_note: The bold black-and-white chequered pattern is unique among British butterflies — nothing else looks like it.
summary: A stunning black-and-white chequered butterfly that looks like no other in Britain. Once you've seen one dancing over purple knapweed on a July afternoon, you'll never forget it.
full_description:
The Marbled White is one of Britain's most unmistakeable butterflies — its bold black-and-white chequered pattern is completely unique. Despite its name it is not related to the white butterflies at all, but belongs to the 'browns' family (Satyrinae), alongside Meadow Browns and Speckled Woods. It loves open chalk and limestone grasslands where it nectars eagerly on purple and pink flowers, especially knapweed, scabious, and thistles — you'll often see several together on a single knapweed flowerhead.

At Old Down, July is Marbled White month. On warm afternoons the hillside can be alive with dozens drifting lazily over the long grass, quite unlike the more jittery flight of other butterflies. Females do something unusual when egg-laying: rather than placing eggs carefully on a foodplant, they scatter them at random while flying, letting the eggs fall into the grass. The caterpillars feed on fine-leaved grasses including Red Fescue and Yorkshire Fog, so the rough, uncut areas of the site are crucial for the colony.

On cloudy days, Marbled Whites roost with wings spread open rather than folded — unusual for the brown family and a useful ID feature. If you find one roosting in the grass, look closely: the underside of the wings has a delicate pattern of grey, white, and black that is just as beautiful as the uppersides.
native_info: Native to southern and central England. A chalk and limestone grassland specialist. Has expanded its range northwards in recent decades, likely in response to climate change.
wildlife_value: Adults are important pollinators of chalk grassland wildflowers, especially knapweed, scabious, and thistles. The caterpillars feed on fine-leaved grasses including Red Fescue and Yorkshire Fog, making rough uncut grassland essential for breeding. A strong population of Marbled Whites indicates that the grassland is being managed well — not cut too early, not too heavily grazed.

life_stages.description: Females scatter creamy-white eggs at random into tall grass while flying — they don't place them carefully on a specific plant. The eggs hatch within 2–3 weeks.

The newly hatched caterpillar does something remarkable: it immediately goes to sleep. It hibernates through autumn and winter without eating, only waking in spring to feed on fine grasses. The caterpillar is green or brown, beautifully camouflaged, and feeds at night — so it's extremely hard to find.
The chrysalis forms in loose soil at the base of grass clumps, or in a thin silken hammock just above the ground. It is pale cream or green, well-hidden in the vegetation.

Adults fly from late June to August, peaking in July. Males and females look similar, though females tend to be slightly larger with more cream in the pattern. Both sexes are avid nectar feeders — look for them on knapweed, scabious, thistles, and marjoram. On cloudy days they roost with wings spread open in the grass.

photos.caption: Marbled White nectaring, showing the bold chequered upperwing pattern
Marbled White at rest on grass showing the underside wing pattern
Marbled White — bold chequered pattern
Marbled White at rest showing underside

confidence_note: The woolly white calyx and clustered flowerheads are distinctive. Flowers are usually yellow but can be orange, red, or cream — look for the fuzzy white 'cushion' around each cluster.
summary: A key chalk grassland plant and the sole foodplant for Small Blue butterfly caterpillars. The clustered flowerheads wrapped in woolly white calyces are unmistakeable once you know what to look for.
full_description:
Kidney Vetch is a low-growing chalk and limestone grassland plant with clusters of small flowers nestled in a distinctive woolly white or cream 'cushion' of sepals. The flowers are usually bright yellow but at Old Down you may also find orange-red or bicoloured forms — the whole plant can look remarkably different from one patch to the next. It grows in short, well-drained turf and is a strong indicator of ancient, unimproved chalk grassland. The leaves are divided into narrow leaflets and have a silvery sheen when young.

Kidney Vetch has one of the most important ecological relationships at Old Down: it is the sole larval foodplant of the Small Blue butterfly (Cupido minimus). The tiny female Small Blue lays her eggs directly on the flower buds, and the caterpillars feed inside the developing seed pods. No Kidney Vetch means no Small Blue — it's that simple. The Six-spot Burnet Moth caterpillar also feeds on it, alongside Bird's-foot Trefoil.

It also fixes nitrogen in the soil through root nodules containing symbiotic bacteria — the same trick legumes use — which helps maintain the low-fertility conditions that chalk grassland wildflowers need. The flowers are a favourite of bumblebees, particularly the short-tongued Buff-tailed Bumblebee which sometimes 'steals' nectar by biting a hole in the base of the flower.
native_info: Native throughout the UK on chalk, limestone, and coastal grassland. Most abundant in southern England.
wildlife_value: The sole larval foodplant of the Small Blue butterfly — one of the most specific ecological relationships in British entomology. Also used as a secondary foodplant by Six-spot Burnet Moth caterpillars and Common Blue caterpillars. The flowers are an important nectar source for bumblebees, solitary bees, and hoverflies. Root nodules fix atmospheric nitrogen, helping maintain the low-fertility soils that chalk grassland specialists need.

life_stages.description: Kidney Vetch forms a low rosette of silky, divided leaves in spring. The leaves have a distinctive silvery-green sheen and feel soft to the touch.

Clusters of small pea-family flowers are held in a thick, woolly white or cream calyx that looks like a cushion. Flowers are usually yellow but can range from cream to deep orange-red. Look at the base of each cluster and you'll see the woolly sepals — this is the clincher for ID.

photos.caption: Kidney Vetch flowerhead showing the woolly white calyx
Kidney Vetch in flower, showing yellow flowerheads

life_stages.description: After flowering, the woolly calyces dry to a papery brown and contain small, kidney-shaped seeds. This is where the plant gets its common name.

similar_species.similarity_note: Both are yellow-flowered legumes of chalk grassland
similar_species.key_difference: Bird's-foot Trefoil has neat, un-woolly flowers and distinctive claw-shaped seed pods. Kidney Vetch always has a thick woolly white or cream calyx around each flower cluster.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Both flower May to September

photos.caption: Kidney Vetch — flowerhead close-up
Kidney Vetch in chalk grassland
Kidney Vetch — orange-red colour form

confidence_note: The inflated yellow-green seed pod rattles audibly when ripe — shake the stem gently. Yellow snapdragon-like flowers and opposite toothed leaves are distinctive.
summary: The gardener of the meadow — Yellow Rattle steals food from grass roots, weakening them and making space for wildflowers to grow. Shake a ripe plant and you'll hear the seeds rattling inside the pods.
full_description:
Yellow Rattle has a clever trick: it is hemiparasitic on grasses, meaning it taps into the roots of nearby grass plants and steals water and nutrients from them. This weakens the grasses, stops them from dominating, and makes space for smaller, slower-growing wildflowers to thrive. It is one of the most important plants in traditional hay meadows and is used deliberately in meadow restoration — sowing Yellow Rattle seed is often the first step in creating a new wildflower meadow.

The plant itself has yellow, two-lipped flowers emerging from an inflated green-yellow calyx, and opposite pairs of toothed leaves. It's annual — it germinates in autumn, flowers the following summer, and dies by August. But the seeds are remarkable: as the plant dries out, the seeds rattle audibly inside the papery inflated pods. This is both the origin of the name and a handy ID feature — shake a plant in July and you'll hear the rattle clearly.

Finding Yellow Rattle at Old Down is a good sign — it indicates the grassland has not been heavily fertilised and is being managed traditionally. It's an indicator of ancient, unimproved grassland that has never been ploughed.
native_info: Native throughout the UK. Most abundant in traditionally managed hay meadows and chalk grassland. An annual that needs bare soil patches to germinate.
wildlife_value: By parasitising grasses, Yellow Rattle reduces grass dominance and creates the diverse, low-fertility sward that supports dozens of chalk grassland wildflowers and the insects that depend on them. The flowers are visited by long-tongued bumblebees, particularly Buff-tailed and Garden Bumblebees. Its decline mirrors the loss of traditional hay meadows — the plant cannot survive in heavily fertilised or frequently mown grassland.

life_stages.description: Yellow Rattle germinates in autumn, producing a small rosette of toothed leaves. It immediately starts parasitising nearby grass roots, even at this tiny size.

The plant grows to 20–50cm, with opposite pairs of toothed leaves and yellow two-lipped flowers emerging from inflated green calyces. Look for the yellow flowers poking out of the swollen pod-like calyx — it looks almost like a tiny snapdragon.

photos.caption: Yellow Rattle flowers — note the inflated green calyx
Yellow Rattle in bloom in a chalk grassland meadow

life_stages.description: By July the flowers fade and the calyces puff up into papery inflated pouches. Inside, seeds loosen from the pod walls and rattle when you shake the plant — give it a try! The plant dies completely after setting seed.

photos.caption: Ripe Yellow Rattle seed pods — shake them to hear the rattle
Yellow Rattle flowers
Yellow Rattle in meadow
Yellow Rattle seed pods

confidence_note: The vivid blue funnel-shaped flowers with protruding red stamens are unlike any other common UK wildflower. Pink buds and blue open flowers often appear on the same plant at the same time.
summary: One of Britain's most striking wildflowers — tall spikes of vivid blue funnels with red stamens poking out. Bees absolutely love it, and the blue is so intense it almost doesn't look real.
full_description:
Viper's Bugloss earns its dramatic name from the spotted stem that can resemble a snake's skin, and the seed that resembles a viper's head. But the plant is completely harmless — in fact, it's one of the best wildflowers you can find for bees, butterflies, and hoverflies. The tall spike of vivid blue, funnel-shaped flowers with long red-purple stamens is one of the most eye-catching sights of summer on chalk grassland. The flowers open pink and turn brilliant blue as they mature — so a single spike carries both colours at once.

It is a biennial: in its first year it produces only a leafy rosette, then in its second year it sends up a tall flowering stem (30–90cm), sets seed, and dies. Look for the rough, bristly leaves with white spots (these are the swollen bases of hairs, not disease) and the hairy, sometimes spotted stem. It favours disturbed and well-drained ground — chalk grassland, roadsides, cliffs, and shingle banks.

Viper's Bugloss is exceptionally rich in nectar and pollen. On a warm day it will be covered in bumblebees, solitary bees, and butterflies competing for the deep nectaries. Even at a distance you can often locate it by the buzzing.
native_info: Native to southern and central Britain. Locally common on chalk, limestone, coastal cliffs, and disturbed ground. Rare in Scotland and Ireland.
wildlife_value: One of the most insect-rich wildflowers in Britain. Produces abundant nectar and pollen accessible to a wide range of bees and butterflies. Particularly valued by long-tongued bumblebees and solitary bees, as well as Small Tortoiseshell and Painted Lady butterflies. Several moth species lay eggs on the leaves. The rough, hairy stems provide shelter for small invertebrates.

life_stages.description: In the first year, Viper's Bugloss produces only a low, flat rosette of rough, bristly leaves. These have distinctive white spots (the bases of stiff hairs) and lie close to the ground through winter.

In the second year, a tall bristly spike grows rapidly to 30–90cm. Flowers open from the bottom upwards — pink buds at the top, vivid blue open flowers below, with red stamens protruding beyond the petals. This gives each spike a wonderful gradient of pink-to-blue.

photos.caption: Viper's Bugloss flowers — vivid blue with protruding red stamens
Viper's Bugloss spike showing pink buds and open blue flowers
Viper's Bugloss in flower
Viper's Bugloss flower spike

confidence_note: The distinctive thyme scent when leaves are rubbed is the clincher. Low, creeping habit with tiny oval leaves and tight clusters of small pink-purple flowers.
summary: The tiniest herb in the chalk grassland — crush a leaf and that unmistakeable thyme scent tells you exactly what it is. The tight mats of pink-purple flowers are a magnet for bees and butterflies.
full_description:
Wild Thyme creeps low across the chalk grassland surface, forming dense, flat mats only a few centimetres high. The tiny oval leaves are aromatic — give one a gentle rub and you'll get that familiar thyme scent immediately. This is the easiest way to confirm the ID. The small clusters of pink-purple flowers are held at the tips of the stems from June to August and are a magnet for bees, butterflies, and hoverflies on warm days.

Wild Thyme (Thymus polytrichus) is the native British species found on chalk and limestone grassland — it's different from the garden thyme (Thymus vulgaris) used in cooking, though they're closely related. It favours very short, well-drained turf where the grass is kept low by grazing or mowing, and cannot compete with tall vegetation. Finding it at Old Down indicates that the short-turf areas are being managed correctly.

Wild Thyme is the larval food plant of the Large Blue butterfly — though that species is not found at Old Down. The plant's main role in the local ecosystem is as a nectar source: it may be tiny, but a mat of flowering thyme on a warm June day will have more insects visiting it per square centimetre than almost any other plant.
native_info: Native to the UK. Found on chalk, limestone, and rocky grassland throughout Britain and Ireland. Requires short, well-drained turf.
wildlife_value: An important nectar source for bumblebees, solitary bees, butterflies, and hoverflies in short chalk grassland. The larvae of several specialist moths feed on Wild Thyme, and it provides shelter for ants and other small invertebrates within its creeping mats. As a plant of short turf, its presence indicates that the grassland has not been over-grown or left unmanaged — it disappears quickly when grass grows too tall.

life_stages.description: Wild Thyme grows as a low, dense mat of tiny oval aromatic leaves, creeping across bare chalk or short turf. In spring it begins to grow new shoots from the woody stems.

photos.caption: Wild Thyme growing as a low mat on chalk grassland

life_stages.description: Small clusters of pink-purple flowers appear at the tips of the stems. The flowers are tiny — only 4–6mm — but a whole mat in flower is highly visible and heavily visited by insects. The aroma is strongest on warm sunny days.

photos.caption: Wild Thyme in flower — pink-purple clusters on chalk grassland
Wild Thyme mat on chalk grassland
Wild Thyme in flower

confidence_note: The lip of the flower mimics a bumblebee so convincingly that it's unmistakeable — there is nothing else like it in the UK.
weather_note: Numbers at any one site vary enormously from year to year — a hillside with dozens one summer may have almost none the next. Likely linked to soil moisture in the preceding autumn.
summary: The most astonishing wildflower in Britain — its lip has evolved to look exactly like a bumblebee, complete with fuzzy texture and patterning. Each flower is a tiny masterpiece.
full_description:
The Bee Orchid is arguably the most extraordinary wildflower in Britain. Each flower has evolved to mimic a female bumblebee in extraordinary detail — the velvety brown-and-yellow lip, the patterning, even the texture, all designed to fool male bees into attempting to mate with it, and in doing so transfer pollen. There's a twist, though: the bee species involved (Eucera long-horned bees) don't live in Britain. So the UK's Bee Orchids are unable to attract pollinators at all — and simply self-pollinate instead. They've kept the disguise but lost the purpose.

Bee Orchids appear first as a flat rosette of oval leaves in autumn, which persists through winter and spring. The flowering spike emerges in June, growing to 15–45cm, and carries 2–7 flowers. The three sepals are pink, and behind them the extraordinary lip — a rounded, velvety lobe coloured warm brown with yellow and cream markings — is unmistakeable. Each flower is a perfect miniature puzzle: the more you look, the more detail you see.

Bee Orchid numbers at Old Down will vary considerably from year to year — some summers may bring dozens, others just a handful. This natural variability is normal and is not cause for concern. They love short, well-drained chalk turf that is not too competitive, and often appear in disturbed ground or near path edges where the sward is kept open.
native_info: Native to southern and central England and Wales. Has spread to disturbed ground and road verges in recent decades. Requires well-drained, low-fertility soil — cannot compete with rank grassland.
wildlife_value: Self-pollinates in the UK (the bee-mimicry attracts no actual pollinators here). However, Bee Orchids are associated with rich chalk grassland ecosystems that support many insects, and their presence indicates the correct management — short, unfertilised turf. The rosette leaves provide shelter for small invertebrates through winter. The flowers produce no nectar, so bees visiting (if they do) get nothing — the orchid is a pure deceiver.

life_stages.description: Bee Orchid spends most of the year as a flat rosette of smooth, oval, grey-green leaves at ground level. These appear in autumn and persist through winter. If you know where Bee Orchids grow at Old Down, look for the rosettes from September onwards — they're easy to find once you know the leaf shape.

The flowering spike emerges rapidly in June, reaching 15–45cm. It carries 2–7 flowers, each with three pink or white sepals and the extraordinary lip that mimics a bumblebee. Look very closely at the lip — you'll see the velvety texture, the 'H' or 'U'-shaped marking, and the overall uncanny resemblance to an insect. After flowering, the plant sets seed and dies back completely.

photos.caption: Bee Orchid in flower — the lip mimics a bumblebee
Bee Orchid close-up showing flower detail
Bee Orchid on chalk grassland, UK
Bee Orchid in flower
Bee Orchid flower close-up
Bee Orchid on chalk grassland

confidence_note: The tight pyramid shape of the flowerhead at the top of the spike is distinctive. Deep pink to bright magenta colour, with unspotted leaves.
summary: One of the most elegant of the chalk grassland orchids — a dense pyramid of deep pink flowers on a tall stem, with a surprisingly strong vanilla and fox scent. Pollinated by moths.
full_description:
The Pyramidal Orchid is one of the easier UK orchids to identify: the dense, rounded pyramid of deep pink to magenta flowers at the top of the stem is distinctive and instantly recognisable. The spike grows 20–50cm and carries dozens of small flowers packed together, opening from the bottom upwards. Each individual flower has a three-lobed lip and two guide ridges that direct visiting insects to the nectar. The leaves are unspotted (unlike Common Spotted Orchid) and grey-green, clasping the stem.

The scent is extraordinary and easy to miss unless you get close — a strange combination of vanilla and fox. This is specifically designed to attract moths and butterflies, which are the main pollinators. On summer evenings, look for moths hovering at Pyramidal Orchid flowers — they hover rather than land, inserting their long probosces for nectar, and pollen masses (pollinia) stick to their eyes or head.

Pyramidal Orchid grows from an underground tuber and reappears each year, though it may disappear for several years if conditions aren't right. Like all native orchids it is protected by law — it is illegal to pick, uproot, or deliberately damage it.
native_info: Native to southern England and Wales. Most common on chalk and limestone grassland. Has spread to road verges and sand dunes, particularly in southern England.
wildlife_value: Pollinated primarily by day-flying butterflies (especially Burnet moths, Common Blue, and Marbled White) and by moths at dusk and night. The flowers produce nectar but the pollen masses stick to visiting insects' heads — an efficient pollination mechanism. The plant is associated with rich chalk grassland communities that support dozens of specialist insects. All native orchids are protected by the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981.

life_stages.description: Through autumn and winter, Pyramidal Orchid exists as a pair of underground tubers, with no above-ground growth at all. The tubers store energy for the following year's flowering.
In spring, unspotted grey-green leaves emerge and clasp the rising stem. At this stage it cannot be confused with Common Spotted Orchid, which has distinctly spotted leaves.

The pyramid-shaped flowerhead is unmistakeable — a tight cone of deep pink flowers that opens from the bottom up. Get close and sniff: the strange vanilla-fox scent is strongest in the evening when moths are active. Each flower has a three-lobed lip and a long spur that contains nectar.

similar_species.key_difference: Common Spotted Orchid has spotted leaves and a more elongated, cylindrical spike that is open at the top. Pyramidal Orchid has unspotted leaves and a tight, rounded pyramid shape.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Common Spotted Orchid flowers slightly earlier (May–June vs June–July for Pyramidal)

confidence_note: Spotted leaves are the key feature — look for dark purple blotches in rings or streaks. Flowers vary from almost white to deep pink-purple, which can cause confusion.
summary: Britain's most common orchid, but no less beautiful for it — pale pink flowers with intricate dotted patterns, and the distinctive spotted leaves that give it its name.
full_description:
The Common Spotted Orchid is the most widespread orchid in Britain, found in a huge range of habitats from chalk downland to woodland rides, road verges, and even garden lawns. The key ID feature is the spotted leaves: each leaf has dark purple blotches, rings, or streaks — no other common UK orchid has this combination of spotted leaves with pale pink flowers. The flower spike grows 20–50cm and carries many flowers, each one a delicate pale pink to deep pink-purple with darker spots and streaks on the three-lobed lip.

The flowers are pollinated by a range of bumblebees and solitary bees, attracted by both the colour and a mild vanilla-like scent. Unusually, the flowers produce nectar (unlike some related orchids that offer nothing and rely on deception). Plants grow from a pair of underground tubers and can live for many years, though they may not flower every season.

Common Spotted Orchid is highly variable: the flower colour ranges from almost white to vivid pink-purple, and the lip pattern varies enormously. This makes identification tricky in some cases, but the spotted leaves are always the clincher. Like all native orchids it is protected by law and should never be picked or uprooted.
native_info: Native throughout the UK. The most common and widespread British orchid. Found in a wide range of habitats but most abundant on neutral to calcareous soils.
wildlife_value: Produces nectar and is pollinated by a range of bumblebees and solitary bees. The flowers are also visited by hoverflies. As a perennial of unimproved grassland, its presence indicates that the site has not been fertilised or heavily disturbed. All native orchids are protected by the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981.

life_stages.description: The spotted leaves emerge before the flower spike, making this the best time to find and identify young plants. Look for 4–8 shiny leaves arranged in a spiral, each marked with dark purple blotches.

photos.caption: Common Spotted Orchid spotted leaves — the key ID feature

life_stages.description: The flower spike rises to 20–50cm with dozens of pale pink to deep pink flowers. Each flower has a three-lobed lip marked with darker pink or purple dots and lines. The spike flowers from the bottom upward, so bottom flowers are fully open while the top is still in bud.

photos.caption: Common Spotted Orchid in full flower, showing the variable pink colouring

similar_species.key_difference: Pyramidal Orchid has unspotted leaves and a tight pyramid-shaped flowerhead. Common Spotted has spotted leaves and a more cylindrical spike.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Common Spotted flowers slightly earlier — May to July vs Pyramidal's June to August

confidence_note: The male is unmistakeable — a brilliant lemon-yellow head and underparts with a chestnut back. Females are streakier but still show yellow. Both sexes have a distinctive chestnut rump in flight.
summary: The brightest bird of the chalk farmland — the male's lemon-yellow head and chest glow like sunshine on the hedgerow. Listen for his song: 'a little bit of bread and no cheeeeese.'
full_description:
The Yellowhammer is one of Britain's most strikingly coloured farmland birds — the male's vivid lemon-yellow head and underparts, contrasting with a rich chestnut back and white outer tail feathers, are unmistakeable. Females are more streaked and less yellow, but still show enough yellow to be distinctive. In flight, watch for the chestnut rump — both sexes have it.

The Yellowhammer's song is one of the most famous in British birdsong: a series of short notes accelerating to a long, thin, buzzing final note, traditionally transcribed as 'a little bit of bread and no cheeeeese.' Males sing persistently from hedgerow tops, fence posts, and scrub from April through July. The call — a sharp 'twick' — can be heard year-round from flocks in winter fields.

Yellowhammers are on the Red List of Birds of Conservation Concern — their population has crashed by over 50% since the 1970s, mainly due to the loss of weedy arable fields and winter stubbles that once provided seeds. Old Down's scrubby chalk grassland, with nearby farmland, is exactly the type of habitat this species needs, making every sighting especially significant.
native_info: Native resident throughout the UK, though rarer in western Scotland and Ireland. Red List species. Population has declined by more than 50% since the 1970s due to agricultural intensification.
wildlife_value: Yellowhammers eat seeds (especially grass seeds and weed seeds) year-round, and feed their chicks almost entirely on insects and caterpillars during the breeding season. They nest low in dense scrub or hedgerow bases, and require uncut field margins and weedy stubble for winter foraging. Their decline mirrors the loss of these traditional farming features.

life_stages.description: The nest is built low in a hedgerow, bramble patch, or tussock of grass — sometimes on the ground. The eggs are pale with distinctive dark scribbly streaks and blotches, as if written in ink, which gives the old folk name 'writing lark.' Clutch size: 3–4 eggs, 2–3 broods per year.
Chicks hatch after about 13 days and fledge around 13 days after that. Both parents feed them almost exclusively on insects and caterpillars, making insect-rich grassland essential in summer.

The male Yellowhammer in summer is one of the most vividly coloured of British birds — brilliant lemon-yellow head and underparts, rich chestnut back with dark streaks. In winter the colours are slightly duller. He sings from exposed perches throughout summer.

life_stages.description: In winter, Yellowhammers form flocks, often mixing with other buntings, finches, and sparrows. They visit stubble fields and weedy margins searching for seeds. The flock includes both males and the duller females and juveniles.

confidence_note: Male in summer has a striking crimson forehead and breast — look for the red patch as the key field mark. Both sexes have a white wing panel visible in flight. Females and winter males are streaky brown and can be confused with other small finches.
summary: A small finch of open countryside — the breeding male has a bright crimson forehead and breast that flash in the sun. Linnets love gorse and bramble scrub for nesting and feed on weed seeds on bare ground.
full_description:
The Linnet is a small, lively finch of heathland, scrub, and open farmland. The breeding male is one of the more attractive British finches: a warm brown back, pale underparts, and a vivid crimson forehead and breast that appear in spring and fade by autumn. The bill is stout and seed-cracking in shape. In flight, white wing panels and white sides to the tail flash conspicuously. Females and non-breeding males are streaky brown and much harder to identify — look for the wing panel as the most reliable feature in all plumages.

Linnets are social birds: you'll often hear them before you see them, giving a rapid, twittering song and a flight call that sounds like a musical 'chichichi.' They nest in loose colonies in dense scrub — gorse, bramble, and hawthorn are favourites — and several pairs may nest close together. The nest is a neat cup of grass and moss lined with hair and plant down.

Like the Yellowhammer, the Linnet is a Red List species whose UK population has declined dramatically. Both are specialist seed-eaters that depend on weedy arable fields, traditional hay meadows, and rough uncultivated ground that modern farming has largely eliminated. Their presence at Old Down indicates that the surrounding landscape still supports a seed-rich food supply.
native_info: Native resident and partial migrant. Widespread throughout the UK but declining. Red List species. Some birds move to coastal areas in winter.
wildlife_value: Linnets feed almost exclusively on seeds — especially the seeds of weeds like fat hen, chickweed, dandelion, and dock. They occasionally take small invertebrates to feed to chicks. Their foraging on bare and disturbed ground can help disperse seeds. As Red List species, Linnets are a priority for habitat management at sites like Old Down.

life_stages.description: In spring and summer the male develops a vivid crimson forehead and breast patch — these are the key ID features. The back is warm brown, the underparts pale. Look for the white wing panel in flight.

photos.caption: Male Linnet in breeding plumage — crimson forehead and breast

life_stages.description: The female is streaky brown with no red colouring — easily confused with other small finches. Look for the white wing panel (less bright than the male's), the small stout bill, and the warm brown tones rather than grey.

photos.caption: Female Linnet — streaky brown with no red

life_stages.description: In autumn and winter, Linnets form flocks, sometimes of hundreds, that roam over farmland and coastal marshes searching for seeds. The males lose their red colouring until spring.

confidence_note: Smooth, shiny, coppery-brown skin with no visible legs, blinking eyes (snakes have no eyelids), and a rounded snout. Much smaller and more slender than any UK snake.
weather_note: Only active in warm weather. Most easily seen on sunny mornings when they bask under flat stones or corrugated metal sheets.
summary: Not a worm. Not a snake. The Slow-worm is a legless lizard — and it's completely harmless. It has eyelids (snakes don't), smooth coppery skin, and a superpower: it can detach its own tail to escape a predator.
full_description:
The Slow-worm is one of Britain's most misunderstood animals. It looks like a snake but is actually a legless lizard — it just lost its legs over millions of years of evolution. You can tell it from a snake because it has eyelids (you can see it blink), ear openings, and a body that is more cylindrical and uniform — snakes have a distinctly wider belly. The skin is smooth and shiny, usually bronze-coppery in males, browner in females (which often have a dark stripe along the back). Both are beautiful in the right light.

Slow-worms are shy and secretive, spending much of their time underground or under cover. At Old Down, look for them under flat stones, pieces of corrugated metal, or in warm grassy tussocks. They are particularly active on warm mornings when they bask briefly before retreating to cover. Their diet is specialised: they eat mainly slow-moving prey that they can catch without a chase — slugs, slow worms (despite the name confusion), small snails, earthworms, and woodlice.

Slow-worms give birth to live young in late summer — unusual for a reptile. The babies are tiny (5–10cm), golden-bronze with a dark back stripe, and look like miniature adults. Like all UK reptiles, the Slow-worm is fully protected by law. If you find one, observe it from a distance — replace any cover exactly as you found it.
danger_note: Slow-worms are completely harmless to people — they cannot bite effectively. However, they are fully protected under Schedule 5 of the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981. It is a criminal offence to intentionally kill, injure, or take a Slow-worm. Please observe without handling.
native_info: Native throughout the UK, including Scotland and Wales. Protected under the Wildlife and Countryside Act 1981. One of the UK's six native reptile species.
wildlife_value: Slow-worms are important predators of slugs and earthworms, making them valuable in gardens and grassland ecosystems. They are preyed upon by Adders, Kestrels, Buzzards, and domestic cats. The eggs of Slow-worm young are a food source for some ground beetles. As a protected species they are an indicator of undisturbed, structurally diverse habitat.

life_stages.description: Baby Slow-worms are born in late summer, usually 6–12 at a time. They are tiny (5–10cm) and strikingly golden or bronze, with a sharp dark stripe along the back and belly. This bold pattern fades as they grow. They are independent from birth.
Adult females are typically brown or bronze-brown, often with a dark stripe along the back and dark sides. They reach 30–50cm in length. Females give birth to 6–12 live young in August–September.

photos.caption: Adult Slow-worm — smooth, coppery skin and blinking eyes distinguish it from snakes

life_stages.description: Adult males are often more uniformly bronze-grey, with fewer dark markings than females. Blue spots may develop on older males — these are thought to be attractive to females. Males can reach 45–50cm, though most are shorter.

confidence_note: Six red spots on metallic blue-green wings — count the spots carefully. Five-spot Burnet has only five spots. The red hindwings are visible in flight.
summary: A day-flying moth that looks like a jewel — metallic blue-green wings with six vivid red spots. It flies slowly in sunshine and doesn't care if you approach closely, because it's actually toxic to birds.
full_description:
The Six-spot Burnet is one of Britain's most distinctive moths, and the only moth you're likely to see flying confidently in bright sunshine. Most moths are night-flying and cryptic — this one is bold, slow, and brightly coloured, because it has nothing to fear. Both the caterpillar and adult moth contain hydrogen cyanide, absorbed from its foodplants, which makes it unpalatable to birds. The vivid red-on-metallic-green colouring is a warning: 'I taste terrible, don't eat me.' This warning colouring is called aposematism.

At Old Down, look for Six-spot Burnets nectaring on knapweed, scabious, and thistles alongside the butterflies in July. They are unhurried and approachable — you can get very close to photograph them. The larvae feed on Bird's-foot Trefoil and Kidney Vetch, so good populations of both plants support good numbers of this moth. The cocoons — papery golden-yellow tubes attached to grass stems — can sometimes be found in late spring.

Mating pairs often stay together for extended periods on flowerheads. The female lays eggs in neat batches on the underside of foodplant leaves. The caterpillar is yellow with black spots and is equally well-defended chemically — birds quickly learn to leave them alone.
danger_note: The moth contains hydrogen cyanide and is toxic if eaten, but is completely harmless to touch or handle. It cannot sting or bite.
native_info: Native throughout the UK. Most abundant on chalk and limestone grassland in southern England. One of several UK Burnet moth species.
wildlife_value: Adults are pollinators of chalk grassland wildflowers, particularly knapweed, scabious, and Bird's-foot Trefoil. The caterpillars feed on Bird's-foot Trefoil and Kidney Vetch, making the presence of both plants important for the species. The chemical defence of both larva and adult means they are not eaten by birds — making them unusual in the food web. Their boldness and slow flight makes them excellent for introducing children to moths.

life_stages.description: Eggs are laid in neat batches on the undersides of Bird's-foot Trefoil or Kidney Vetch leaves. They are pale yellow and hatch within 2–3 weeks.

The caterpillar is fat, yellow-green with black spots. It feeds on Bird's-foot Trefoil and Kidney Vetch. The caterpillar overwinters in a state of reduced activity and resumes feeding in spring. Like the adult, it contains hydrogen cyanide and is left alone by birds.

In late spring, the caterpillar spins a papery, golden-yellow or white cocoon high up on a grass stem or plant stalk. These are distinctive and can be found by careful searching. The cocoon is elongated and pointed at both ends.

Adults emerge in late June and fly through August. The metallic blue-green forewings with six vivid red spots are unmistakeable. Adults fly slowly in sunshine and frequently visit flowers to nectar. They are completely approachable — their toxic chemistry means they have no need to flee.

confidence_note: Orange and black banding with double narrow black bands on the abdomen — the double bands are the key feature that separates it from many similar hoverflies. Much smaller and more slender than a wasp.
summary: One of Britain's most familiar hoverflies — orange and black striped, hovering perfectly still in mid-air before darting to a flower. It looks like a wasp but has no sting. Millions migrate here from mainland Europe every year.
full_description:
The Marmalade Hoverfly is probably the hoverfly most people have noticed — hovering motionless, then darting sideways, then hovering again. The orange and black banding mimics a wasp or bee well enough to deter many predators (this is called Batesian mimicry), but it is completely harmless. Look closely and you'll see the single pair of wings (flies have two wings; wasps and bees have four), the large fly-style eyes, and the short antennae — nothing like a wasp's.

Marmalade Hoverflies are migrants — every year, millions fly north from southern Europe and Africa to take advantage of the UK's summer flowers. Some years bring enormous numbers; on good days you can see them streaming in off the coast. Adults feed on nectar and pollen from flowers, while the larvae are voracious predators of aphids — a single larva can eat hundreds of aphids before pupating, making hoverflies important natural pest controllers.

The hover is extraordinary — the hoverfly maintains a fixed position in space with wingbeats of 120 per second, making tiny rapid adjustments for wind and air currents. It's one of the most impressive flying skills in the insect world. To see it best, watch one hovering over a flower on a warm, still afternoon.
danger_note: Despite resembling a wasp, hoverflies cannot sting. They are completely harmless.
native_info: Native to the UK and a migratory visitor in large numbers from mainland Europe. One of the most common hoverfly species in Britain.
wildlife_value: Adults are important pollinators — they visit a very wide range of flowers and can pollinate species that bees ignore. Larvae eat aphids, making hoverflies valuable natural pest controllers in gardens and crops. Migratory species like this one link ecosystems across Europe — the same individual may pollinate flowers in Spain, France, and England in a single season.

life_stages.description: The larva is a pale, slug-like maggot found among aphid colonies on plant stems. It is completely blind and moves by feel, but can eat hundreds of aphids. It pupates in a brown barrel-shaped pupa on or near the foodplant.

The adult is seen hovering over flowers or resting on leaves in sunshine. The orange and black banding is bright and contrasting. In flight, the hover is its most distinctive behaviour — it can hang motionless for extended periods, then dart sideways at speed.

Marmalade Hoverfly on flower

similar_species.key_difference: Bumblebees are large and very furry; hoverflies are smaller and sleek. Bumblebees have four wings and longer antennae. Hoverflies hover motionless; bumblebees rarely do.
similar_species.time_of_year_note: Both visible spring to autumn

confidence_note: Brown with cream or pale yellow spots, including a distinctive row of eye-spots near the wing edges. The dappled-shade habitat and habit of basking in patches of sunlight is a strong clue.
summary: The butterfly of dappled sunlight and woodland edges — warm brown with cream spots, and a habit of spiralling upward in fierce territory battles. One of the few UK butterflies that can be seen in every month from March to October.
full_description:
The Speckled Wood is a medium-sized brown butterfly with a distinctive pattern of pale cream spots on a warm dark-brown background, and a row of small eye-spots around the wing edges. It is strongly associated with dappled shade — woodland rides, hedgerows, and scrubby edges where patches of sunlight filter through to the ground. Males defend individual spots of sunlight on the ground or a leaf, rising in spiralling aerial battles with rival males before one retreats and the winner returns to his sunlit patch.

Speckled Wood is one of the longest-season butterflies in Britain — you can see it in every month from March to October in a warm year. This is partly because it has multiple broods, and partly because it can overwinter as either a caterpillar or a chrysalis — uniquely flexible among British butterflies. The caterpillars feed on a range of grasses and are bright green with cream stripes, perfectly camouflaged on a grass blade.

At Old Down, look for Speckled Wood along the edges where scrub or hedgerow meets the open grassland. Adults bask with wings open or half-open on sunny leaves, and are remarkably easy to approach when basking.
native_info: Native throughout England, Wales, and southern Scotland. Has expanded its range northward significantly in recent decades. One of the more common and widespread UK butterflies.
wildlife_value: Caterpillars feed on a range of coarse grasses (Cock's-foot, Yorkshire Fog, False Brome), making areas of long grass at woodland and scrub edges important for breeding. Adults take nectar from bramble, ragwort, and other flowers. The species rarely visits open grassland flowers but is an important link between woodland-edge and grassland habitats.

life_stages.description: Bright green with a pale stripe, perfectly camouflaged on a grass blade. May overwinter as a caterpillar — the only UK butterfly that can overwinter in two different life stages (as either caterpillar or chrysalis).

Adults bask with wings spread in dappled sunlight. The pattern of cream spots and eyespots on dark brown wings is distinctive. Males rise in fierce spiralling chases to defend sunlit patches. Multiple broods mean adults can be seen from March to October.

confidence_note: Male is unmistakeable — white with bright orange wingtips. Female is white with black wingtips and often confused with the white butterflies. Both sexes have a beautiful green-and-white marbled pattern on the underside of the hindwing.
weather_note: A true spring butterfly — numbers and timing vary with spring weather. Cold springs push emergence back; warm springs bring them out in April.
summary: The arrival of the Orange-tip is one of the classic signs that spring has truly arrived. The male's bright orange wingtips are unmistakeable — look for them dancing along hedgerows and wildflower verges in May.
full_description:
The Orange-tip is a spring butterfly — it emerges in April and May and is typically gone by June, with just a single brood per year. The male is one of the most distinctive British butterflies: white wings with a large patch of vivid orange at the tip of each forewing. There's no mistaking him when he flies past. The female is white with dark wingtips and no orange — she is regularly confused with Small White or Green-veined White, but the beautiful marbled green-and-white underside of the hindwing (visible when at rest or in flight) is present in both sexes and is the clincher.

The caterpillars feed on the flowers and seed pods of Garlic Mustard (Alliaria petiolata) and Cuckooflower (Cardamine pratensis) — plants that are usually found in damp meadows, hedgerow bases, and woodland edges rather than dry chalk grassland. At Old Down, look for Orange-tips flying along the hedgerow edges and in areas where damp ground or rank vegetation supports these foodplants.

One of the most remarkable things about Orange-tip caterpillars is that they are cannibalistic — if two caterpillars meet on the same plant, one will eat the other. This is why the female lays only a single egg per plant: if she laid more, they'd just eat each other.
native_info: Native throughout England, Wales, and southern Scotland. Common and widespread where foodplants grow. A single brood, flying April to June.
wildlife_value: Orange-tips are pollinators of spring wildflowers, including Cuckooflower and Garlic Mustard. The caterpillars feed on these plants' seed pods, making them dependent on damp, undisturbed ground where the plants grow. The adults are important nectar visitors to early-flowering plants including Bluebell, Dandelion, and Cuckooflower — all at a time when few other butterflies are flying.

life_stages.description: The female lays a single bottle-shaped egg on the flower stalk of Garlic Mustard or Cuckooflower — crucially, only one egg per plant, to prevent cannibalism. The egg starts white and turns orange as it develops, which can help you spot it.

The caterpillar is green-grey, almost perfectly matching the seed pods it feeds on. It is cannibalistic — if it meets another Orange-tip caterpillar, it will eat it. Look carefully along the seed pods of Garlic Mustard in June.

The chrysalis is remarkable — long, curved, and pointed, shaped like a curved thorn or leaf midrib. It is extremely well-camouflaged and attached along a stem. The butterfly overwinters inside and emerges the following April.

The male is brilliant white with a large orange patch covering the outer third of the forewing tip. Both sexes have a beautiful marbled green-and-white underside on the hindwing that looks like crinkled lichen — a perfect camouflage when at rest.

confidence_note: Male is brilliant sulphur yellow — the most vivid yellow of any UK butterfly. Female is a very pale greenish-white and can be confused with Large White, but the distinctive leaf-shaped wing outline and orange spot on each wing identify both sexes.
weather_note: One of the earliest butterflies of the year — can emerge on warm days in January or February. Emergence timing varies with winter temperature. Often the first butterfly of the year.
summary: The canary-yellow male Brimstone is one of the most vivid sights of early spring — often the first butterfly of the year. The word 'butterfly' may actually come from this species: 'butter-coloured fly.'
full_description:
The Brimstone is one of Britain's longest-lived butterflies — adults live for up to 13 months, overwintering as adults tucked into ivy or Holly, and emerging on the first warm days of late winter or spring. On a mild February afternoon, a flash of vivid sulphur yellow along a hedgerow is the classic first-Brimstone-of-the-year moment. The male is the most intensely yellow butterfly in Britain — nothing else comes close. The female is a pale, almost white greenish-cream and is regularly mistaken for a Large White at first glance.

Both sexes have a distinctive wing outline — the wings are shaped like leaves, with a small hook at the tip of the forewing. When at rest with wings closed, the leaf-vein pattern and leaf-green colouring of the underside makes both sexes effectively invisible against ivy or leafy vegetation. An orange spot sits at the centre of each wing, visible on both surfaces.

The caterpillars feed exclusively on Buckthorn and Alder Buckthorn — neither of which is particularly common at Old Down, so Brimstones seen there are likely adults that have moved in from nearby woodland or hedgerow rather than being bred on site. Adults are powerful fliers and can travel significant distances.
native_info: Native throughout England and Wales; scarce in Scotland. Requires Buckthorn or Alder Buckthorn for breeding. Adults are long-lived and mobile.
wildlife_value: As one of the earliest butterflies to appear in spring, Brimstones are early pollinators of spring flowers — they particularly favour Primrose, Lungwort, and Bugle. The caterpillars are entirely dependent on Buckthorn species. The overwintering adults' leaf-shaped, leaf-coloured wings are a remarkable example of camouflage adaptation.

life_stages.description: The caterpillar is plain green with a white stripe along the side — perfectly camouflaged on a Buckthorn leaf. It feeds on Buckthorn (Rhamnus cathartica) or Alder Buckthorn (Frangula alnus). It pupates in a leaf-shaped green chrysalis attached to a stem.

The male is brilliant sulphur yellow — possibly the origin of the name 'butterfly' (butter-coloured fly). Each wing has an orange central spot. The leaf-shaped outline is apparent at rest, and when wings are closed the green underside makes him nearly invisible.

confidence_note: Unmistakeable: black wings with bold red bands and white spots at the wingtips. No other UK butterfly has this combination.
summary: One of Britain's most familiar and beautiful butterflies — jet black with bold red bands and white spots. Often one of the last butterflies seen in autumn, feeding on fallen fruit and ivy flowers.
full_description:
The Red Admiral is one of the most striking and recognisable British butterflies. The bold combination of jet black wings with bright red bands crossing the forewings and hindwings, plus white spots near the forewing tips, is completely unmistakeable — there is nothing else like it in the UK. Underneath, the wings have a beautiful complex pattern of brown, black, and orange that provides excellent camouflage when roosting on tree bark.

Red Admirals are primarily migrants from southern Europe and North Africa — vast numbers move north each spring, and the British population is reinforced by these arrivals each year. Some individuals are now known to overwinter successfully in southern England, emerging on warm winter days. The caterpillars feed on Stinging Nettles, making any patch of nettles in a sunny, sheltered spot potentially important for breeding.

In late summer and autumn, Red Admirals are drawn to ripe and rotting fruit — orchards, blackberries, fallen windfall apples, and garden ivy flowers are magnets for them at this time of year. They bask with wings spread flat in the autumn sunshine, soaking up warmth before their long flight south. At this time, they can also be seen roosting motionless on sun-warmed fence posts, tree trunks, and walls.
native_info: Resident and migrant. Breeds in the UK using Stinging Nettles, but many individuals are migrants from mainland Europe. Increasingly overwinters in the south of England.
wildlife_value: Caterpillars feed on Stinging Nettles, making nettles a key resource for this species. Adults are important pollinators of late-season flowers — especially ivy flowers in autumn, which are one of the most important late nectar sources for many insects. Red Admirals are among the most mobile of UK butterflies, linking habitats across large distances.

life_stages.description: The caterpillar lives in a tent of folded nettle leaves, sewn together with silk. It is black or dark brown with yellow spots along the sides. Peel back a folded nettle leaf on a sunny nettle patch in summer and you may find one.
The chrysalis hangs from a stem near the nettle patch, dark brown with small metallic-gold patches.
Fresh adults in summer are vividly coloured — jet black, red, and white. They nectar on a wide range of flowers including knapweed, thistles, bramble, and marjoram.

confidence_note: Smooth, silver-grey bark is distinctive — like an elephant's leg. Oval leaves with slightly wavy edges and silky hairs when young. Triangular nuts in prickly cases (beech mast).
summary: The most graceful of British trees — smooth silver-grey bark, a soaring straight trunk, and a canopy that turns copper-gold in autumn. Beech woodland at Old Down is one of the most magical habitats on the site.
full_description:
Beech is a tree of superlatives. Its bark is the smoothest and most silver-grey of any British tree — people can't resist touching it, and unfortunately can't resist carving initials into it either, which is why so many old beeches carry old love-carvings that stretch and distort as the tree grows. The canopy is dense and domed, and the leaves emerge in spring as the most delicate, translucent pale green — then turn deep glossy green in summer, and finally copper, orange, and gold in autumn. Old beech trees in autumn are one of the best sights in the British countryside.

Beech casts such dense shade that almost nothing grows beneath it — the woodland floor is often bare brown leaf litter. This is sometimes called a 'beech desert,' though it is not truly dead: fallen leaves rot slowly and the deep leaf layer provides habitat for fungi, invertebrates, and small mammals. In autumn, beech produces triangular nuts called mast, held in spiky four-lobed husks. In a mast year (heavy seed production, which happens every few years), the woodland floor can be carpeted with them. Wood mice, Grey Squirrels, Chaffinches, and even Badgers gorge on them.

The smooth bark is a favourite surface for Nuthatch and Treecreeper to search for insects. Look for the distinctive screw-shaped holes where woodpeckers have been working, and feel the bark for the tiny channels and bumps where fungi are fruiting. Beech is native to southeast England and parts of Wales but was widely planted across Britain in the 18th and 19th centuries.
native_info: Probably native to SE England and parts of Wales; widely planted elsewhere. A dominant tree of chalk and limestone woodland in southern England.
wildlife_value: Beech mast is a vital high-calorie food for squirrels, mice, voles, pigeons, and Chaffinches in autumn and winter. The dense leaf litter supports a rich fungal community, including mycorrhizal fungi that live on beech roots. Smooth bark is searched by Nuthatch and Treecreeper for invertebrates. Old beech trees develop cavities used by bats and hole-nesting birds.

life_stages.description: In April–May, beech buds are the most elegant of any tree — long, pointed, and copper-brown, like tiny cigars. As they burst, the new leaves emerge pale green and translucent, edged with silky white hairs. Look up through a newly leafed-out beech canopy against a blue sky for one of the great sights of spring.

life_stages.description: By summer the leaves are deep glossy green and the canopy is dense. The smooth silver-grey bark and tall, straight trunk are the best ID features at any time of year.
