confidence_note: Britain's largest beetle — up to 7.5cm long including the male's enormous antler-like mandibles. Shiny dark brown to black body with red-brown wing cases. Females are smaller and have much smaller mandibles. Unmistakeable.
weather_note: Most active on warm evenings in June–July. Males fly at dusk looking for females, making an impressive buzzing flight.
summary: Britain's largest and most spectacular beetle — the male's enormous antler-like mandibles look fearsome but are actually used to wrestle other males, not to hurt people. The larvae spend up to seven years eating rotting wood underground before becoming the beetle you see.
full_description:
The Stag Beetle is the largest beetle in Britain and one of its most dramatic insects. The male's extraordinary mandibles — enlarged jaws resembling a stag's antlers — are used exclusively in combat with other males for the right to mate with females. They look terrifying but can only very rarely pinch a finger, and even then it is not painful. The females have much smaller, functional jaws.

The adult beetles live for only a few weeks and do not feed as adults (they may sip tree sap or fruit juice). The real life is underground: the larvae spend 3–7 years feeding on rotting wood — old tree stumps, buried roots, and dead wood in soil. This long larval period in rotting wood makes the Stag Beetle entirely dependent on old trees and dead wood habitat. Loss of old trees and over-tidying of gardens and woodlands has reduced populations significantly — the Stag Beetle is a UK Priority Species.

Males fly at dusk in June and July, making a distinctive loud buzzing flight as they cruise low over the ground searching for females. It's an incredible sight. If you find one on the ground, move it gently to the nearest piece of old wood or log pile — do not move it far from where you found it.
danger_note: The male's antler-like mandibles look alarming but are almost always too weak to pinch meaningfully. Handle with care if you must, but they are harmless and should not be feared.
native_info: Native to Britain. UK Priority Species — has declined significantly due to loss of dead wood habitat. Mainly southern England.
wildlife_value: Stag Beetle larvae are major decomposers of dead wood, breaking down old tree stumps and buried roots. This decomposition is essential for woodland soil health. Adults are eaten by Foxes, Badgers, and crows. The species depends entirely on the presence of old trees and dead wood — a Stag Beetle population is a reliable indicator of long-established woodland or veteran trees.

summary: The most dramatic beetle in Britain — when threatened it curls its tail up like a scorpion and opens its fangs. Completely harmless to people, but a ferocious predator of slugs, worms, and other invertebrates.
full_description:
The Devil's Coach Horse is a rove beetle (family Staphylinidae) — a family characterised by very short wing cases that leave most of the abdomen exposed and flexible. This gives the Devil's Coach Horse a scorpion-like appearance, especially when threatened: it raises the tip of its abdomen upward, opens its large, powerful jaws, and releases a foul-smelling chemical from glands at the tail tip. This defensive display is dramatic but entirely harmless to people.

The Devil's Coach Horse is a nocturnal predator, hunting under logs, stones, in leaf litter, and along garden paths at night. It eats slugs, worms, fly larvae, and other invertebrates — making it a genuine garden and woodland ally. It moves fast and purposefully, and can bite if handled carelessly (its mandibles are surprisingly strong), though the bite is no worse than a small pinch.

In Irish folklore, the Devil's Coach Horse was believed to be a manifestation of evil and could supposedly absorb sins by chewing them. Medieval Europeans thought it could curse people with a glance. In reality it is one of the most beneficial beetles in the garden.
danger_note: The defensive display (raised abdomen, open jaws) looks alarming but is harmless. The bite from the large mandibles is a mild pinch only. The chemical secretion from the tail tip smells unpleasant but is not toxic. Do not handle unnecessarily.
native_info: Native throughout Britain and Ireland. Very common in a wide range of habitats.
wildlife_value: An important nocturnal predator of slugs, worms, fly larvae, and other invertebrates. Significant in controlling slug populations. The larvae are also predatory, living in soil and leaf litter.

life_stages.description: Look under logs, stones, and in leaf litter. At night it hunts actively on paths and in hedgerow bases. confidence_note: Yellow and black banded abdomen, narrow waist, and smooth (not fuzzy) body. Four wings. The yellow face has a characteristic anchor or dagger-shaped black mark — use this to distinguish from German Wasp (which has three dots). In flight, legs hang down.
summary: Wasps are misunderstood — all summer they are ferocious hunters of caterpillars and flies, doing a huge amount of pest control. Only in late summer, when the colony collapses and workers go sugar-seeking, do they become a nuisance. They sting only in defence.
full_description:
The Common Wasp has an image problem. Most people associate wasps with late-summer nuisance — crawling over jam sandwiches, buzzing aggressively around picnics, and stinging unprovoked. But this behaviour happens only for a few weeks at the end of the colony's life. From April to August, wasps are beneficial predators: they catch caterpillars, flies, aphids, and other insects by the thousand to feed their larvae, doing enormous amounts of pest control in gardens and crops.

A Common Wasp nest is a masterpiece of engineering. Starting from scratch each spring, the queen builds a nest from chewed wood fibre (paper) — she chews bark and dead wood, mixes it with saliva, and applies it as a paste that dries to a papery material. Workers expand the nest through summer until a colony may contain 10,000 workers. The hexagonal cells are used for raising larvae.

In late summer, the new queens and males are produced, the colony collapses, and the workers — suddenly without larvae to feed — look for sugar instead. This is when they become a nuisance. Stay calm near wasps, cover food and drink, and resist swatting — a crushed wasp releases an alarm pheromone that makes nearby wasps aggressive.
danger_note: Wasps sting in self-defence when they feel threatened. The sting is painful but not medically significant for most people. However, some people are allergic to wasp venom — a severe allergic reaction (anaphylaxis) is a medical emergency. People with known allergies should carry an EpiPen.
native_info: Native throughout Britain and Ireland. Very common everywhere.
wildlife_value: A major predator of caterpillars, flies, aphids, and other insects in summer — providing significant pest control. Wasps also act as pollinators of some flowers and fig species. Nest wood-pulp building recycles dead wood. Wasp nests are raided by Badgers and Green Woodpeckers for the larvae.

Workers (sterile females) hunt insects to feed the larvae and expand the nest. In late summer, look for workers feeding on ripe fruit, sap runs, and any sweet food source as the colony winds down.

summary: The world's most famous pollinator — and a fascinating social insect. A single colony can contain 60,000 bees. Honey Bees communicate the direction and distance of flowers to each other by dancing.
full_description:
The Honey Bee is one of the most important insects on Earth — responsible, alongside other pollinators, for the production of a third of all human food. A single colony can contain 50,000–60,000 workers, all daughters of a single queen. The colony works as a single superorganism: workers build wax comb, raise larvae, collect nectar and pollen, guard the entrance, and regulate the temperature of the hive by fanning their wings.

Honey Bees communicate the location of flowers using the 'waggle dance' — a figure-of-eight dance performed inside the hive in which the angle of the waggle run relative to vertical indicates the direction of the food source relative to the sun, and the duration of the waggle indicates distance. This is one of the most sophisticated communication systems known in the animal kingdom.

The Honey Bee's sting is barbed — it stays in the skin after a sting, and the venom sac continues to pump venom for up to a minute. The bee dies after stinging. Remove the sting promptly by scraping (not squeezing) it out. Honey Bees are gentle compared to wasps — they sting only to defend the colony or themselves when pressed. Managed hives are kept by beekeepers; wild colonies nest in tree holes, old roofs, and other cavities.
danger_note: The sting is barbed and stays in the skin — scrape it out immediately (don't squeeze the venom sac). Sting is painful but not dangerous for most people. People with bee venom allergy should carry an EpiPen.
native_info: Native to Britain; the managed race (Apis mellifera mellifera) has been kept by beekeepers for thousands of years. Also present as wild colonies in tree holes and old buildings.
wildlife_value: One of the most important pollinators of wildflowers and crops. A colony visits millions of flowers per day. Honey Bee wax and honey support other wildlife; wax moth larvae feed in old combs. Swarms are eaten by opportunistic predators.

weather_note: Only sings in warm sunshine — a cool cloudy day will produce silence even in peak season. The song is warmth-dependent.
summary: Close your eyes on a warm August afternoon at Old Down and listen — that rapid chirping from the grass is the grasshopper's song. Males rub their hind legs against their wings to 'stridulate'. Grasshoppers are ancient: they've been singing like this for 300 million years.
full_description:
The Common Field Grasshopper is the most frequently heard grasshopper on dry chalk grassland in southern England. On a warm, still August afternoon at Old Down, their song — a series of short, buzzy chirps, each burst lasting 1–2 seconds, repeated every few seconds — is one of the defining sounds of the site. To produce it, the male rubs a row of tiny pegs on his inner hind femur against a hardened vein on the forewing — a process called stridulation. Different grasshopper species produce different songs; with practice they can be identified by ear alone.

Grasshoppers belong to a group called Orthoptera, which also includes crickets. The key difference: grasshoppers have short antennae (shorter than the body), are active by day, and produce song by rubbing leg against wing. Crickets have very long antennae, are mostly nocturnal, and produce song by rubbing the wings together. Grasshoppers have been on Earth for over 300 million years — they were singing on ancient fern forests long before the dinosaurs existed.

The Common Field Grasshopper is highly variable in colour — the same species can be brown, green, purple, or striped. This polymorphism may help individuals match their specific patch of ground. Adults overwinter as eggs laid in soil, with nymphs hatching in May and reaching adulthood by July.
native_info: Native throughout Britain. The most common grasshopper on dry chalk and limestone grassland in England.
wildlife_value: Grasshoppers are an important food source for Kestrel, Skylark, Yellowhammer, and many invertebrate predators including spiders and ground beetles. Their grazing helps maintain short-turf structure. Chalk grassland grasshopper populations are indicators of site quality.

life_stages.description: Nymphs hatch in May from overwintered eggs in soil. They look like miniature adults but with developing wing buds and no adult wings. They moult several times as they grow.

Adults reach full size by July. On warm sunny days, males sing from prominent grass stems. Try to spot one singing — watch for the rapid up-down movement of the hind leg. The song stops immediately if the grasshopper spots you approaching.

summary: A beautifully speckled green cricket found on bramble and hedgerow from late summer. Almost flightless, it calls at such a high frequency that most adults can barely hear it — a bat detector brings its song into earshot.
full_description:
The Speckled Bush Cricket is one of the most beautifully marked insects in Britain. Bright green, covered in a dense constellation of tiny dark purple-brown speckles, it looks like a leaf flecked with dew. The extremely long, thread-like antennae distinguish it immediately from grasshoppers. It is found on bramble, hedgerow shrubs, and rough vegetation from late July through to November.

The song is produced by wing-rubbing (stridulation), but unlike grasshoppers, crickets rub their wings together rather than leg against wing. The Speckled Bush Cricket calls at around 20–30kHz — at the very top edge of most adults' hearing range, and completely inaudible to anyone over about 40. Children often hear it as a very faint, high-pitched tick; adults typically need a bat detector set to 20–25kHz to detect it. Bring a detector on an evening walk in August and the hedgerows will be full of invisible crickets.

Females have a long, curved, sabre-shaped ovipositor (egg-laying tube) that sticks up behind the abdomen — this makes them easy to distinguish from males. The species is almost entirely flightless, spending its life climbing slowly through vegetation. Eggs are laid into bark crevices and overwinter.
native_info: Native throughout England and Wales. Common in hedgerows and scrub.
wildlife_value: Speckled Bush Crickets are eaten by bats (which detect them easily), spiders, and insectivorous birds. They eat pollen, plant material, and small invertebrates.

confidence_note: Round, often brownish abdomen with a distinctive white cross or diadem of white spots on the top. Females are much larger than males. Builds a classic circular orb web with a spiral of sticky thread. Sits in the centre of the web, or hides in a retreat at the edge connected by a signal thread.
summary: The architect of the most beautiful structure in nature — the orb web, rebuilt every day. The dew-covered web on a September morning is one of Britain's iconic sights. Spiders are not insects — they have 8 legs and two body parts, not six legs and three.
full_description:
The Garden Spider builds one of nature's most impressive structures: a near-perfect circular orb web with a spiral of sticky thread radiating out from a central hub. The spider typically rebuilds this web every day or two — consuming the old web to recycle the protein, then spinning a new one in the small hours of the morning. A web may contain 20–60 metres of silk. On dewy September mornings, hundreds of webs glitter across hedgerows and grassland at Old Down.

The Garden Spider is a spider, not an insect — an important distinction to make with children. Spiders have 8 legs (insects have 6), two body parts — cephalothorax and abdomen — (insects have three), and fangs (chelicerae) rather than jaws. The Garden Spider's bite is not medically significant in the UK — it could theoretically pierce skin but almost never does, and the venom is not dangerous to people. They are completely harmless.

Females grow much larger than males over the summer, reaching 10–13mm by autumn compared to the male's 4–8mm. After mating in autumn, females lay a silk egg sac containing 300–900 eggs, often hidden in a crevice or under bark. The female dies after the first hard frost; the eggs overwinter and hatch in spring.
native_info: Native throughout Britain and Ireland. Very common everywhere.
wildlife_value: An important predator of flying insects including flies, wasps, moths, and beetles caught in the orb web. Garden Spiders are eaten by Blue Tits, Robins, and other insectivorous birds. The webs also trap many non-pest insects, but the ecological net effect is positive as a predator.

They sit in the centre of the web waiting for prey, or hide in a curled leaf at the edge connected by a signal thread. September morning dew reveals dozens of webs in hedgerows.

confidence_note: Flat, fast-moving, shiny brown-orange arthropod with 15 pairs of legs (30 legs total). The first pair of legs are modified as venomous fangs. Much flatter and faster than a millipede. Found under stones and logs. Antennae and legs about the same length.
summary: The fastest animal under a log — centipedes sprint across the ground the moment you lift a stone. They are predators: the first pair of legs are modified into fangs. Not dangerous to people, but great to watch.
full_description:
Centipedes are ancient, fascinating, and completely harmless to people in Britain. The Brown Centipede (Lithobius forficatus) is the most commonly encountered species — flat, shiny, reddish-brown, about 2–3cm long, with 15 pairs of legs (exactly 30 legs). It moves with surprising speed when a stone is lifted, scurrying for cover. This speed is essential: centipedes are hunters, chasing and catching invertebrate prey using their speed and modified front legs.

The front pair of legs in centipedes has evolved into venomous fangs (forcipules) used to seize and paralyse prey — primarily insects, worms, and other invertebrates. In theory the fangs can pierce human skin, but in practice this almost never happens with British species, and even if it did, the sensation would be no worse than a mild bee sting. British centipedes are entirely harmless to handle.

A useful distinction for children: centipedes have ONE pair of legs per body segment and are flat, fast predators. Millipedes have TWO pairs of legs per body segment, are rounder, much slower, and eat dead plant material. Lift a log and you may find both; the centipede sprints, the millipede ambles.
native_info: Native throughout Britain and Ireland. Very common everywhere under logs, stones, and in leaf litter.
wildlife_value: An important predator of soil invertebrates, insect larvae, worms, and slugs. Centipedes are eaten by Robins, Blackbirds, Hedgehogs, Shrews, and many other predators. They are a key part of the soil food web.

confidence_note: Grey, armour-plated crustacean with 14 legs and two short tail appendages. When touched, the Pill Woodlouse (Armadillidium vulgare) rolls into a perfect ball. Common Woodlouse (Oniscus asellus) is flatter and cannot fully roll up. Both found under logs, stones, and damp material.
summary: Not an insect, not a spider — woodlice are actually crustaceans, more closely related to crabs and shrimps than to beetles. The pill woodlouse rolls into a perfect ball when touched. They breathe through gills, not lungs.
full_description:
The woodlouse is one of the most reliably findable creatures on a wildlife walk — lift almost any log, stone, or piece of bark in a damp spot and you'll find them. But woodlice are not insects. They are crustaceans — the same group as crabs, shrimps, and lobsters — and are one of the very few crustaceans to have adapted to life on land. They still breathe through gills, not lungs, which is why they need damp conditions: their gills must stay moist to function.

The most common species found in chalk grassland and woodland edge are the Pill Woodlouse (Armadillidium vulgare) — which rolls into a perfect sphere when disturbed, like a tiny armadillo — and the Common Woodlouse (Oniscus asellus), which is flatter, slightly shinier, and cannot fully roll up. Counting legs is useful: woodlice always have 14 legs (7 pairs), plus two tail-like uropods.

Woodlice are completely harmless and important decomposers — they eat dead plant material, helping break it down into nutrients. They are eaten by spiders, centipedes, ground beetles, shrews, and toads.
native_info: Native throughout Britain. Very common in damp habitats everywhere.
wildlife_value: Important decomposers of dead plant material — they break down leaf litter, dead wood, and organic debris, releasing nutrients back into the soil. Eaten by spiders, centipedes, ground beetles, shrews, toads, and slow-worms.

weather_note: Most active at night and after rain. In dry weather they seal their shell opening with dried mucus (aestivation) and wait for moisture.
summary: Two types to look for at Old Down — the familiar large Garden Snail on vegetation, and the beautiful colourful Banded Snails on chalk grassland. The banded snails are especially interesting: the colour and band pattern vary from snail to snail, even in the same patch.
full_description:
Old Down is home to two distinct groups of snails worth knowing about. The Garden Snail (Cornu aspersum) is the familiar large snail — mottled brown with a thick, globular shell — common on vegetation, paths, and in hedgerow bases. It is the classic 'snail with a shell' of the British garden and countryside.

More interesting ecologically are the banded snails (Cepaea species) found on chalk grassland. White-lipped Snail (Cepaea hortensis) and Brown-lipped Snail (Cepaea nemoralis) are both beautiful, colourful snails whose shells vary dramatically in colour and banding: yellow, pink, or brown, with anywhere from zero to five dark bands. This variation is genetic — it is one of the most studied examples of visible evolution in real time. The colour and banding pattern affects survival (camouflage against different backgrounds) and body temperature (darker shells warm up faster in cold conditions).

Snails are molluscs — related to slugs, mussels, and octopuses. Their muscular 'foot' glides on a carpet of mucus, leaving the silver trail. In dry weather they seal the shell opening with dried mucus and wait. In winter they hibernate under leaf litter. Song Thrushes are specialist snail predators, smashing shells on a favourite 'anvil' stone — look for a stone with broken shell fragments as a sign that a Song Thrush regularly hunts nearby.
native_info: Garden Snail is native/naturalised throughout Britain. Cepaea snails are native chalk grassland species.
wildlife_value: Song Thrushes are specialist snail predators — their distinctive 'anvil' behaviour (smashing snail shells on a favourite stone) is one of the clearest signs of a healthy snail population. Hedgehogs, Badgers, and ground beetles also eat snails. Chalk grassland Cepaea snails are an important food source for Song Thrush and are indicators of chalk grassland quality.

life_stages.description: Most active at night and after rain. In daytime find them resting under leaves, on walls, or sealed with dried mucus waiting for rain. After rain, walk the paths and look for the silver trails leading to snails feeding on low vegetation.

summary: The most delicate and beautiful grass on the chalk — Quaking Grass trembles constantly in the breeze, its heart-shaped spikelets dancing like tiny lanterns. Finding it confirms you're on genuinely old, never-fertilised grassland.
full_description:
Quaking Grass is one of the most distinctive and beautiful grasses in Britain, and one of the most reliable indicators of ancient, unimproved chalk grassland. It grows in rosettes of flat basal leaves, sending up flowering stems in June and July that carry clusters of small, flattened, heart- or egg-shaped spikelets on hair-fine branching stalks. The spikelets are purplish-green, about 6–9mm across, and the slightest movement of air sets them trembling and quaking — catching the light and appearing to dance. In a gentle breeze, a patch of Quaking Grass is one of the most enchanting sights in British grassland.

As an ancient grassland indicator, Quaking Grass tells you something important about Old Down: this has been grassland for a very long time, without ploughing or heavy fertilisation. It is a slow-growing perennial that cannot re-establish on recently disturbed or fertilised ground. Wherever you find Quaking Grass, you're standing on a piece of landscape history.

Dried stems with spikelets retain their shape and movement for months — they have been used in dried flower arrangements for centuries. The folk name 'totter grass' also refers to the trembling motion.
native_info: Native throughout Britain and Ireland on chalk and limestone grassland. An ancient grassland indicator species.
wildlife_value: The seeds are eaten by seed-eating finches including Linnet and Yellowhammer. The dense tussock structure provides shelter for grassland invertebrates. Most importantly, Quaking Grass indicates the presence of high-quality, ancient chalk grassland that supports a rich community of specialist plants and animals.

confidence_note: Pinnate leaves with pairs of small round toothed leaflets. Crush a leaf and it smells strongly of cucumber — the most reliable ID. Round flower heads on long stems: top half red (female flowers), bottom half yellow-green (male flowers). Very common on chalk.
summary: The best fun plant on the chalk — crush a leaf of Salad Burnet and smell your fingers. It smells exactly like cucumber. An ancient chalk grassland indicator that was eaten in salads and herb gardens for centuries.
full_description:
Salad Burnet is one of the most engaging plants to show children on the chalk. It looks modest at first — pairs of small round toothed leaflets arranged along a central stem — but crush a leaf between your fingers and the smell is immediate and striking: fresh cucumber, unmistakeable and pleasant. This smell is what made Salad Burnet a popular salad herb in Tudor and medieval times; Francis Bacon recommended it for garden paths because 'it perfumes the air most delightfully, being trodden on and crushed.'

The flowers are unusual. Each small round flower head has a two-part structure: the top half bears the red female flowers (which receive pollen), while the lower half bears the drooping yellow-green male flowers (which release pollen). Wind carries pollen from the male flowers upward to the female flowers above. Watch carefully on a breezy day and you can see the male flowers releasing their pollen in clouds.

Like Quaking Grass, Salad Burnet is an indicator of ancient, unimproved chalk grassland — it colonises slowly and can't re-establish on disturbed or fertilised ground quickly. Its presence at Old Down is a sign of the site's age and the quality of its management. It grows low and keeps growing even when grazed or cut — the leaf rosette survives close cutting and produces new growth.
native_info: Native throughout England on chalk and limestone grassland. An ancient grassland indicator.
wildlife_value: Salad Burnet flowers are wind-pollinated but also visited by small insects. The leaves are eaten by rabbits and some invertebrates. As an ancient grassland indicator, its presence at Old Down confirms the quality of the chalk grassland for other specialist species.
